paragraphs: Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation into the relationship between co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang and a businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence agencies are said to view as a Chinese spy, CNBC reported. In an email to staff on Sunday, Huang said he had an affair with the woman and apologized.

According to reports in The New York Times and the Financial Times, as cited by CNBC, U.S. intelligence agencies have expressed concern that the woman, Alice Huang, has been passing information to Beijing. She is affiliated with a cloud company and Nvidia customer called Megaspeed. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," Huang wrote.

Nvidia's board said it would examine the allegation that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. It said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised," but that its inquiry "will examine all available information." A company spokesperson said Huang was committed to continuing as CEO without interruption.

The story lands amid a U.S.-China trade dispute over artificial intelligence. The U.S. restricts exports of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips to China, though it has approved certain older, slower models. Megaspeed has been accused of helping restricted Chinese companies acquire Nvidia chips, and Nvidia representatives previously said the company had already been investigated for evading export controls. Huang has pushed for broader chip exports to China, arguing it is better for the U.S. if the world builds on American technology.

Several dates are coming up. Three House Republican committee chairs sent Huang a letter on Wednesday asking him to attend a closed-door briefing with lawmakers on Nov. 18. Nvidia reports third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17 and holds a major conference in Washington at the end of the month.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said Sunday he is "a hard yes" on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the BBC reported. Speaking on ABC's This Week, Jeffries said Hegseth had "abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran." He added, "Pete Hegseth has got to go."

The push comes from Rep. Thomas Massie, an outgoing Republican and critic of President Donald Trump, who has said he plans to introduce an impeachment resolution as early as Monday. According to the BBC, it contains eight articles, including an accusation that Hegseth violated the War Powers Resolution of 1973 through U.S. involvement in the Iran war.

The Pentagon told the BBC it had followed the law and that Hegseth would not be deterred by "phony investigations." In a video last week urging Congress to approve the Pentagon's latest budget request, Hegseth called the effort "sham articles" and said it was part of "the politics of personal destruction." He said, "Didn't work against President Trump and it won't work with me."

Jeffries is the favorite to become House Speaker when Democrats take control in January. The BBC said he has described a role for Democrats as a check on the administration, but House Democrats are not currently focused on impeaching Trump.

On the numbers, the BBC reports Democrats hold a 254-seat House majority with some races uncalled, well above the 218 needed to pass articles of impeachment. Removal would require a two-thirds Senate majority, which Democrats are not expected to have. Congress returns to session this week.

White House Deputy Chief of Staff Richard Walters is leaving the Trump administration, Fox News reported, following President Donald Trump's decision to replace chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller. Walters is described as a longtime ally of Wiles.

Miller confirmed the departure in a statement to Fox News, calling Walters an "invaluable member" of the White House who has helped deliver some of the administration's biggest victories and who will keep helping from the outside. According to LegiStorm, Walters was appointed to the deputy role in May 2026. Georgetown University says he previously served as executive director of the inaugural committee for Trump and Vice President JD Vance.

Fox describes the exit as the first major staff turnover as Miller prepares to install his own leadership team when he takes over Monday. It is part of a broader effort by Trump to overhaul his administration after the midterm elections, in which Republicans lost control of both the House and the Senate. Trump named Miller to the job on Friday, calling him one of his "most trusted advisors." A White House official told Fox that the change was "very amicable" and that Wiles submitted her resignation Thursday night.

Separately, Miller's wife, Katie Miller, said Sunday that she will stop recording new episodes of The Katie Miller Podcast. In a post on X, she said the time commitment was too great and that nothing is more important than raising their four children. She said two episodes already recorded will still be released.

The White House and the Department of Homeland Security say they will not change course on immigration enforcement after last week's midterm defeat, according to the BBC. In a statement, the White House said the administration "will not slow down its efforts to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens." A DHS spokesperson told CBS that "ICE is NOT backing away or slowing down."

The BBC reports that exit polls ranked immigration as the third most important issue for midterm voters, behind the economy and the state of democracy. Multiple U.S. officials told CBS that the administration blames its losses on concerns about the economy, affordability and the war with Iran rather than its immigration crackdown. ICE sources told CBS that officials have been told to aim for about 2,700 arrests a day, up from an earlier target of 2,000.

Vice President JD Vance had appeared open to adjustment after the results, writing that he was open to changing enforcement by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor. The BBC says the White House posture appears to have hardened after Trump promoted Stephen Miller, widely seen as the architect of the administration's hardline immigration policy, to chief of staff on Friday.

The Guardian reports that Miller's promotion has stoked expectations that Trump will double down on the crackdown and refuse concessions to the new Democratic majority in Congress. Dan Eberhart, a Trump donor, told Reuters it signals a "fighting-from-a-bunker approach" for the last two years.

The BBC notes that enforcement sweeps this year prompted protests in cities including Chicago, Minneapolis and Los Angeles, and that two protesters, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were fatally shot by immigration agents in Minneapolis.

Democrat Mary Peltola leads Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by 637 votes in Alaska's uncalled Senate race, according to Fox News. Peltola has 48.17% support, and the state has not released new vote tallies for days. Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, said on a radio program Sunday that the result may take days or weeks.

Dunleavy called the state's voting system "very confusing" and said a big batch of votes should arrive on Friday, Nov. 13, and another on Wednesday, Nov. 18. Under ranked-choice rules described by Fox, if no candidate has 50% of first-choice votes by Nov. 25, the count moves to rounds that reallocate second and third choices. A ballot measure to repeal ranked-choice voting was also on the ballot, and Fox reports the "no" side leads narrowly at 51.85%, with that question also too close to call.

Dunleavy also discussed what has been called the "Decoy Dan" matter. He said a second candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan, was placed on the ballot in what he described as an alleged plot to siphon votes from the incumbent. He said the state division of elections found the candidacy not legitimate and declined to list him, but the state Supreme Court ruled against the division and he went on the ballot. Dunleavy said that he was reopening the investigation after a New York Times report tied possible knowledge of the scheme to Peltola's campaign, and that the Department of Justice is also investigating. Fox did not report a response from the Peltola campaign to those claims.
Dunleavy said officials are looking at possible wrongdoing, including anything resembling perjury or misrepresentation of a candidate's intent.

Democrats made sweeping gains in state legislatures across the country in Tuesday's election, NPR reported, with stations in North Carolina and Arizona describing what that could mean. NPR noted that Republicans dominated state elections in 2010 and used that power to advance their agenda for more than a decade.

In North Carolina, Republicans have held what they call working supermajorities for much of the past decade, letting them override most vetoes by Democratic governors. Colin Campbell of WUNC said that allowed abortion restrictions, expanded private school vouchers and gerrymandered congressional maps. Democrats flipped the state House with a comfortable majority. One Senate race is still being counted and could leave Republicans with a one-seat majority or a tie, which the Democratic lieutenant governor would break. If Democrats control both chambers, Campbell said, that could mean a rollback of abortion restrictions. If not, it is unclear what would get done. Gov. Josh Stein has urged both parties to cooperate on issues like affordability.

In Arizona, Democrats will hold both chambers and the governor's office for the first time since 1966, according to Wayne Schutsky of KJZZ. Gov. Katie Hobbs set a state record of more than 500 vetoes. Schutsky said Democrats are expected to try to crack down on the state's school voucher program. Republican state Sen. John Kavanagh acknowledged that his party missed an opportunity to address voter concerns about the vouchers, though Republicans told Schutsky their losses had more to do with President Trump.

Nationally, Republicans held 28 legislatures going in and Democrats 18. The National Conference of State Legislatures projects Democrats will control 25 and Republicans 21. New Democratic trifectas include Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota and Nevada.

A Republican Texas lawmaker is urging Gov. Greg Abbott to call a special session to limit the governor's emergency powers before Democrat Gina Hinojosa takes office, Fox News reported. State Rep. Brian Harrison made the request publicly on Wednesday, after Hinojosa defeated Abbott in Tuesday's election. She is set to take office in January 2027.

Harrison wrote on X that Republicans "still have total power in Texas" for the remaining ten weeks and should use it to "restore separation of powers." He also said he believes governors should not have unchecked emergency powers regardless of party, and he pointed to a bill, HB911, that he filed in December 2022. He told Fox he first demanded the change in 2022 and argued that the powers are unconstitutional.

Fox reports that under Section 433.002 of the Texas Government Code, the governor may issue and amend emergency directives during a declared emergency, subject to the law's requirements. Under the Texas Disaster Act of 1975, disaster declarations must be renewed after 30 days and the Legislature can end them at any time. The Texas Tribune reported that Hinojosa pledged on the campaign trail to declare a "high-cost emergency" and issue executive orders to halt gas and diesel taxes and freeze residential electricity rates. She said on X her administration will "lead with a politics of courage, not convenience."

Fox said Abbott's office and Hinojosa's campaign did not respond to its request for comment. Abbott told supporters he would help her team during the transition. The Houston Chronicle reported that some Republican state senators have pledged to "hold the line" against Democratic policy goals.

Democratic gains in the midterms have opened a path to activating the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact before the 2028 presidential race, Fox News reported. Democrats now hold the governor's office and both legislative chambers in Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Nevada.

The compact has been enacted by 18 states and Washington, D.C., representing 222 electoral votes, which is 48 short of the 270 needed to take effect. Fox reports that the four states' combined 50 votes would bring the total to 272, and Arizona could push it to 283 if Democrats win both of its chambers. The nonprofit National Popular Vote says it has identified sponsors in each state and expects bills before or early in the 2027 sessions. If the compact takes effect, member states would award electors to the national popular vote winner, leaving the Electoral College in place formally.

The legal question is disputed. Patrick Rosenstiel of National Popular Vote told Fox that Article II, Section 1 gives states exclusive power over awarding electors, and that the only credible question is whether Congress must consent. Hans von Spakovsky of Advancing American Freedom, a former Federal Election Commission member, argued the compact is unprecedented and that the Supreme Court would likely reject it. He said it requires congressional approval under the compact clause, which he thinks a Democratic Congress would grant, and that non-participating states would have grounds to sue.

On timing, Rosenstiel said the compact would apply in 2028 only if states representing at least 270 electoral votes join by July 20 of that year. Until then, Fox notes, the Electoral College remains unchanged.

UK Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said the government is "looking seriously" at adding Vinted and eBay to the list of platforms that children under 16 would be barred from using, "to keep children safe." She was speaking on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme.

The Sunday Times had earlier reported that the ban was being expanded to the second-hand marketplaces because of fears that messaging functions let strangers groom children. According to the newspaper, the similar platforms Depop and Facebook Marketplace would also be included.

Both companies responded. eBay said the details of the proposed legislation were not yet clear and that it looked forward to "understanding more" and working constructively with the government. Vinted said it welcomed "open dialogue" with ministers and the regulator. It said direct messaging is "part of how the platform works" but that it has "zero tolerance for harmful or explicit content." eBay requires members to be over 18, while Vinted is aimed at adults but lets parents or guardians create supervised accounts for children.

The wider ban, announced in June, is due to start in March next year and will cover 10 of the biggest platforms, including Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat. YouTube will be covered, though YouTube Kids will not. A full list has not been published, but the government said it would cover services "whose purpose is to enable social interaction and which allow users to post material." Roblox will not be banned, although features such as chat will be restricted.

Matthew Sinclair of the Computer and Communications Industry Association, which represents tech firms, urged ministers to avoid "scope creep," saying a messaging restriction would reach services families rely on to stay in touch. Rani Govender of the NSPCC said the "real question" was how to make age checks effective. Ofcom set out its recommendations on age checks last month.

Bailiffs acting for Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) reportedly raided the Dutch offices of Chinese carmaker BYD and seized digital records, according to the Sunday Times, as cited by The Guardian. The raids are said to have taken place in August at Schiedam and Hoofddorp.

They came before a court case in The Hague this week, which will decide whether BYD has a case to answer over allegations that its Ti7 SUV infringes intellectual property rights linked to the Land Rover Defender. The Times reported that JLR suspects BYD reverse-engineered some technology that could be used in the Ti7, and wanted to secure the records before they could be destroyed. JLR and BYD both declined to comment on the "ongoing legal proceedings."

Motoring experts have compared the seven-seat plug-in hybrid to the Defender since it went on sale in China in September last year. BBC Top Gear magazine called it the "Chinese Defender clone." BYD is due to launch it in the UK in January at £47,995, more than £20,000 below the Defender. JLR's Defender 110 starts at £68,465. JLR, which is owned by India's Tata Motors, sold 29,500 Defenders to retail customers between July and September, up from 25,370 a year earlier.

The Guardian noted that JLR has fought copycat claims before. In 2019 it won a case to stop Jiangling Motor Corporation selling a similar vehicle, after a three-year court battle. It has also worked with Chinese firms, forming a joint venture with Chery in 2012.

Chery's Jaecoo model, which sits outside that venture and has been called the "Temu Range Rover," was the UK's bestselling car in October with 10,813 registrations, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders. Range Rover sales fell to 43,300 in the third quarter from 47,196 a year earlier.

Amazon has assembled a new team working on what it calls a "new-to-world robot product" for the home, according to a CNBC analysis of job posts. The effort comes even though some owners of Amazon's earlier home robot, Astro, believe its days are numbered.

Jeff Bezos pushed the project in 2017, convinced consumers would soon have a robot at home. Astro, essentially an Alexa-equipped tablet on wheels that can navigate a home, recognize faces and act as a roving security monitor, was unveiled in 2021 at $1,450. It never moved beyond an invite-only product and shipped to just a few thousand customers. A business version launched in 2023 and was shut down less than a year later.

Emily Lugo Velez, who has had an Astro in North Carolina since 2023, told CNBC she feels "stuck with it" and expects to send it to the "trash heap" when it dies. She still uses it to check on pets and appliances. Ken Washington, Amazon's former VP of consumer robotics, said Bezos seemed disappointed with Astro's lack of functionality.

This year Amazon redeployed much of the Astro team and, in March, acquired New York-based Fauna Robotics, maker of a 3.5-foot humanoid called Sprout. Fauna became part of a new Personal Robotics Group. A since-removed job listing said robots were "about to step out of the movies and into our homes." It is unclear what product the group is building.

An Amazon spokesperson said the company is "committed to tackling the challenges that can unlock the personal robotics category," while noting a substantial gap between labs and living rooms. Barclays forecast in January that the humanoid market, now valued at $2 billion to $3 billion, could reach roughly $40 billion by 2035.

A large randomized trial found that intensive training of 911 dispatchers, first responders and community members did not improve survival with a favorable neurologic outcome after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. The results were presented at the American Heart Association's scientific sessions and published in the New England Journal of Medicine, according to STAT.

About 350,000 people in the United States have a sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital each year, and only 1 in 10 survive. STAT reports that survival chances drop by 10% for every minute without CPR.

Starting in 2021, researchers assigned 60 North Carolina counties, home to about 8.5 million people, to intensive education or standard practice. Dispatchers were trained to recognize cardiac arrest and guide bystanders through CPR, first responders were taught to use defibrillators, and workplaces, religious groups and government offices received CPR training. Over five years, 22,459 adults had a cardiac arrest outside hospital.

Lead author Carolina Malta Hansen said survival "remained low and unchanged" despite a high-quality trial. An exploratory analysis found bystander CPR rose in the fourth year, and she argued that a longer, more intense effort deserves study. Only about 5% of the population was trained, she said, compared with about 80% in Denmark, where CPR certification is required for a driver's license. She cited Denmark's survival of about 16% versus about 10% in the US.

Amrish Deshmukh of the University of Michigan, who was not involved, called the results disappointing but not surprising, noting that many interventions have not improved survival. Brahmajee Nallamothu suggested that starting as Covid-19 emerged may have delayed the effects, and asked whether the educational approach was right.

Physicists have used electrical noise to show that electrons in a copper-based superconductor form pairs well before the material superconducts, according to Ars Technica's report on a Science study. The team was led by Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University.

Cuprates were found in the late 1980s to superconduct at temperatures reachable with liquid nitrogen, yet physicists still disagree on why. At the center of the debate is the pseudogap, a state in which electrons seem to go missing above the superconducting temperature. One explanation is that the electrons are frozen into patterns such as charge density waves, with superconductivity arising separately. The other is that the electrons are missing because they have formed pairs.

The researchers measured shot noise, tiny fluctuations from individual charges arriving in a current. Allan likened it to rain on a roof: if electrons arrive in pairs, the drops are effectively heavier and the noise rises. Using a scanning tunneling microscope on crystals of a cuprate called BSCCO, cooled to a few degrees above absolute zero, they tuned the energy of the electrons by adjusting voltage. Extra noise, the sign of pairing, appeared right at the local pseudogap energy and held across samples with different chemistry.
To rule out other noise sources, they applied magnetic fields of up to six tesla, which suppresses pairing. The noise fell toward the single-electron level, as expected if pairs caused it.

The measured pairing energy was well above the temperature at which the material superconducts. Swart said the picture is of pre-formed pairs, with phase coherence, where electrons move together as a fluid, setting in only at lower temperatures. That suggests the bottleneck is getting pairs to move together, not getting electrons to pair.

A group of young mathematicians has resolved Graham's rearrangement conjecture, a question posed in 1971 by Ronald Graham, according to a story first published by Quanta Magazine and republished by Wired. The final paper, by Lisa Sauermann of the University of Bonn and Huy Tuan Pham of the University of Chicago, appeared in February 2026, closing the problem after a proof spanning four papers.

Graham was a noted mathematician and a past president of both the American Mathematical Society and the International Jugglers' Association. His question asks whether a set of different nonzero integers can always be rearranged so that every running total, from the first two numbers, the first three and so on, is different. In juggling terms, it means ordering throws so that no two balls land on the same beat.

The answer is clearly yes when all numbers are positive, and was already known to be yes when positives and negatives are mixed. Graham asked about numbers wrapped around a clock that repeats after a prime number, p, where some sums can equal zero. He conjectured the answer was still yes, but for decades no one could prove it.
Noga Alon of Princeton credited "the power of collaboration, the power of the young generation, the power of probabilistic methods."

Alp Müyesser of Oxford and his former adviser Alexey Pokrovskiy of University College London tackled sets containing nearly every number up to p. They set aside a few chosen numbers, randomly ordered the rest, and used the spares to fix any stretch that summed to zero. They posted this in 2022, within a paper on a more general problem. Later, Noah Kravitz of Oxford, unaware of that work, found the conjecture in an online archive of unsolved problems.

NASA has opened its $1 million Moon Base Student Challenge, announcing it Sunday during a MAX POWER event at Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida. The competition invites student teams at U.S. high schools and post-secondary schools to contribute designs for the Moon Base.

NASA says it is building a Moon Base where astronauts will live, work and explore in the lunar South Pole region, and that a permanent human presence there paves the way for future crewed missions to Mars. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said the agency is looking for students ready to think creatively, work as a team and take on real problems connected to its future on the Moon.

The multiphase challenge asks teams to design solutions in six categories: power generation and storage, construction, life-support systems, surface mobility, communications networks, and astronaut safety. NASA says the deliverables reflect industry skills, such as trade studies, concept proposals and stakeholder briefings. It says participants on technical, vocational and various academic tracks can take part without prior specialized engineering or technical experience.
Teams must register through the NASA STEM Gateway, and registration is open until Jan. 25, 2027. NASA directs participants to its website for full rules and eligibility requirements.

Carlos García-Galán, manager of the Moon Base Program, said students bring the bold ideas NASA is seeking. Elaine Ho, associate administrator for the Office of STEM Engagement, said she was excited to see the creativity the challenge spurs. The Office of STEM Engagement designed the challenge with the Moon Base Program, and the Institute of Competition Sciences administers it under a contract with NASA's Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovation.

Antipersonnel mines are returning to the battlefield in Ukraine, according to New Scientist. When 122 countries signed the Ottawa Treaty in 1997 to ban them, the weapons seemed to be on the way out. Explosive ordnance disposal consultant Seán Moorhouse says three technologies have enabled their resurgence: 3D printing, microcontrollers and drone delivery.

New Scientist describes two forms of mine. Blast mines, weighing 100 grams or less, are typically scattered by aircraft and are pressure-activated, designed to maim. Larger fragmentation mines, laid by combat engineers, spray lethal fragments in all directions. With 3D printing, any frontline unit can make its own mines, in varied shapes and colours. Some, like the curved, green Caterpillar, blend in with vegetation, while urban mines may resemble brick or concrete.

Microcontrollers connected to sensors can replace tripwires. The most common type in Ukraine, nicknamed Jonik, or “little soldier,” is magnetic and sensitive enough to be set off by a nearby rifle. Other mines use Doppler microwave sensors to detect movement, or sense body heat or vibration. A new variety is triggered by the approach of any Bluetooth device.

Drones can place both types of mine precisely on tracks and paths or around trenches, which gives a greater chance of finding a victim than random scattering. Human rights organisations and a UN commission have reported that Russian forces are using drones to drop antipersonnel mines to target civilians in Kherson. The article does not include a Russian response.

The article says networks of soldiers and volunteer groups make mines in garage workshops in Ukraine and Russia. Roy Gardiner of Defense Tech for Ukraine says any group with access to explosives can rapidly produce such devices. Ukraine has suspended its implementation of the treaty, and Poland, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia are pulling out, which Moorhouse says suggests mines have some utility.

Moorhouse says demining agencies must update their training and awareness programmes urgently. AI-enabled drones are beginning to help with detection and disposal, but he warns the risk is growing and that many states and non-state actors are likely to adopt these weapons despite the human cost.

Gadi Eisenkot, Israel's former military chief and leader of the Yashar party, began the task of forming a government on Sunday after President Isaac Herzog formally gave him a mandate. The Guardian says he has 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension. Al Jazeera describes the window as six weeks.

In the October 27 election, Eisenkot's bloc won 48 of the 120 parliamentary seats and Netanyahu's camp won 53. Neither reached the 61 needed for a majority. Al Jazeera reports that Arab-led parties won a record 19 seats, and both Arab-majority lists endorsed Eisenkot during consultations with Herzog.

Eisenkot said Israel was in a state of emergency, approaching a "point of no return", and called for a national emergency government. He appealed to Netanyahu's Likud and to Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich's party to join, but only with himself as prime minister. The Guardian quotes him saying his "door is open and my hand is extended".

The pages differ on the Arab-led parties. The Guardian says Eisenkot has set conditions for any Arab party joining, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish state, and that his partner Yisrael Beiteinu has said it will not join such a coalition. Al Jazeera says he has ruled them out. It adds that winning the two ultra-Orthodox parties would give him exactly 61 seats, though they demand military exemptions that his bloc opposes.

Netanyahu called on Saturday night for a national unity government with Eisenkot, but it is unclear whether they could agree. The Guardian reports he has claimed the election was "stolen" by Arab parties, offering little evidence. Herzog and the Central Elections Committee say the vote was valid. Al Jazeera notes Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister, and if Eisenkot fails he would likely be next to get the mandate, with fresh elections possible after that.

European officials will attend this week's U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine in the United Arab Emirates, France's foreign minister said Sunday. Jean-Noël Barrot told French radio that France "will be there and will ensure that Europe's voice is heard." He did not say who would represent Paris, or whether European officials would take part in the negotiations or only observe.

The Kremlin had said otherwise. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov argued that a three-way format between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv had already been agreed, and accused European governments of failing to decide who speaks for them. He also acknowledged that security talks would eventually need Europe's involvement.

The Abu Dhabi meetings are set for Tuesday and Wednesday. According to NPR, this is the fourth round brokered by the Trump administration and the first since Geneva in February. Earlier rounds made little progress, and the U.S. war with Iran reduced the chances of a breakthrough. Envoy Steve Witkoff has said the agenda will cover postwar security arrangements, de-escalation and humanitarian issues.

Russia's delegation will again be led by Vladimir Medinsky and will for the first time include two deputy foreign ministers and senior military officials. NPR says this could signal readiness to address harder questions, but the Institute for the Study of War suggested some of the same officials have previously slowed talks. The gaps remain wide: Russia demands Ukraine give up large parts of its territory and renounce NATO membership, while Zelenskyy wants security commitments spelled out.

President Trump said a coming agreement "might involve all of Europe." Zelenskyy said he had not been given details and called the prospect "dangerous." Fighting continues, and he said Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles at the Kyiv area overnight Saturday, with four intercepted.

Iran has executed three men accused of carrying out armed unrest during January's anti-government protests, according to state media. Hassan Dioband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh were accused of throwing Molotov cocktails and grenades, using bladed weapons and firearms, and setting fire to public facilities in the city of Karaj, west of Tehran, Iran's state news agency Tasnim reported.

Tasnim said the executions followed the Supreme Court upholding their convictions for "participating in operational activities on behalf of the Israeli Zionist regime, the United States and hostile groups". The alleged damage included an electricity substation in Karaj that caused power outages in some areas. Dioband was arrested on January 11, and ten others accused of taking part under his supervision were later arrested. Reuters reports they received prison terms of 5 to 10 years.

The BBC says the executions are the latest in a series linked to the protests, including those of people accused of ties to Israel and the United States. Executions in Iran have increased since U.S.-Israeli strikes on the country began in late February.

The protests began in December over the high cost of living and grew into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on January 8 and 9. Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths and blamed the violence on "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the U.S. and Israel. Foreign-based NGOs gave higher figures, and the BBC said it received multiple accounts from Iranians of security forces opening fire on unarmed protesters.

UN human rights chief Volker Türk said in August that at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since March 19, including 27 in cases linked to the protests. Amnesty International says Iran executed at least 2,159 people last year, the highest figure on record since 1981.

Polish prosecutors have opened a terrorism investigation after a 24-year-old man opened fire in Kraków's busy market square on Saturday afternoon, killing six people and injuring 17. The Guardian reports that authorities said the attack was probably inspired by far-right ideologies. Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday.

Police said the suspect, a Polish national named in local media as Michal O, drove into the square at about 3pm wearing military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest, and shot at random. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński said he was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held "very radical" and "ultra-nationalistic" views. He was wounded in an exchange of fire with police and taken to hospital under heavy guard. Police also confirmed that his parents and sister were found dead at the family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, probably from gunshot wounds.
The dead include three Polish women, a 51-year-old Austrian woman and a 32-year-old British man. Five of the wounded are foreign nationals from Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal and Russia.

Two police officers were injured while pursuing and detaining him. Police arrived 23 seconds after the first emergency call. Jakub Kulik was critically hurt and Artur Morański was shot in the chest. Both were reported to have come out of medically induced comas on Sunday. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said they "probably saved many human lives", and the justice minister said their actions prevented further casualties.

The attack has shaken a country long seen as safe. Officials had already linked several school stabbings in October to extremist content online. Leaders including Zelenskyy, Macron, Merz and Meloni expressed condolences, and security was bolstered in Warsaw.

Seven people were killed and more than 100 injured on Sunday when two trains collided in the al-Ayyat district of Giza province, about 30 miles south of Cairo, according to officials cited by the Guardian and the BBC. The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.

According to the transport ministry, a train travelling to Fayoum crashed into the rear of a Cairo-to-Aswan train. An inspection indicated the Aswan train had been stationary on the same track. Several carriages derailed and fell down an embankment, and images showed overturned carriages, one apparently split in two. The ministry confirmed that the driver of one train was among the dead.

Health minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said patients were being treated for broken bones and head injuries. The government said hospitals nearby were on heightened alert. A local resident, Ayman Gamal, said he saw about 80 of the injured taken away by ambulance and that some passengers trapped in a carriage of the stationary train died. The Egyptian Red Crescent said it was giving aid and psychological support at the scene.

President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered an investigation into the circumstances and that anyone found to have been negligent be held accountable. Trains between Giza and Upper Egypt were suspended while cranes cleared the wreckage, and the railway authority has not said how long that will take.

The BBC reports calls in Egypt on Sunday for the transport minister to resign. The Guardian says derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance, despite government modernisation plans. The crash was near the site of the country's deadliest rail disaster, a 2002 fire in which more than 370 people were officially reported killed.

Pope Leo XIV arrived in Argentina on Sunday, where President Javier Milei and his sister Karina Milei, the presidential secretary, greeted him at Jorge Newbery airport near Buenos Aires. It is the first papal visit to the country in nearly four decades, since John Paul II in 1987. The pope came from Uruguay, the first stop on a 12-day, three-country tour that ends in Peru.

Al Jazeera and NPR both describe tension between Milei's government and the Argentine Catholic Church over austerity. Milei has cut social spending, and NPR reports health spending has fallen 48 percent in real terms. The church has criticised the measures, and some clergy have joined protests. Milei has defended the cuts as necessary to control inflation and, NPR says, reach a budget surplus. NPR also reports the church has criticised his embrace of artificial intelligence, a technology Leo has warned poses threats to humanity.

Milei's relationship with the late Pope Francis, an Argentine who never visited his homeland as pope, was contentious. Al Jazeera says Milei called him a "communist" and an "imbecile who defends social justice". Karina Milei has said the government regards the trip as purely religious and that the pope "belongs to all Argentines."

Leo's schedule includes a welcome ceremony at Plaza San Martin and a meeting with Milei at the Casa Rosada. He will also visit a prison and celebrate Mass in Buenos Aires, Luján and Córdoba province before leaving Wednesday. Al Jazeera notes that Catholics in Argentina fell from 71 percent of the population in 2013-2014 to 58 percent a decade later, according to Pew.

New Zealand faces weeks of uncertainty after Saturday's election gave neither the right nor the left a decisive win, NPR reports. Negotiations over a very narrow governing majority look like the only route to power for either side. Parties will not begin talks until final results are released on November 27.

On election night's count, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's center-right National party appeared close to the slimmest possible return to power, by one seat. Luxon did not claim victory but expressed cautious optimism about negotiating a second term, and he leads a caretaker government. Chris Hipkins' center-left Labour appeared to fall short of a majority, though it remained hopeful.

The vote was a rebuke to both major parties. National won 29.21 percent of the party vote and 42 seats, all from local races. Labour won 29.36 percent but only 36 seats. Minor parties gained: libertarian ACT won 13 seats, populist New Zealand First 12, the Greens 16 and Te Pāti Māori five. A new group, Opportunity, led by political newcomer Qiulae Wong, won seven seats. Wong has said she could work with either side. With 131 lawmakers elected so far, 66 seats are needed for a majority.

Electoral officials began counting nearly 400,000 special votes, including from New Zealanders abroad, a process expected to take three weeks. These have historically given left-wing parties an extra seat or two, which could take the thin majority from the right, though NPR says the left would likely still struggle to form a government. If no government can be formed, New Zealand could face a fresh vote. Several senior National ministers would leave politics on current results.

The Cop31 UN climate summit opens Monday in Antalya, Turkey, with leaders and representatives of close to 190 countries attending. The Guardian reports that Australia, which presides over the formal negotiations under a compromise on competing bids, wants a result that delivers progress. Australia's climate minister Chris Bowen said: "We need a tangible outcome focused on implementation that people can see is real."

The talks take place against what the Guardian describes as the strongest El Niño on record, intensified by fossil fuels. It reports that temperatures this year have passed the 1.5C Paris limit. Friction is expected between rich and poor countries over who pays for climate impacts and over the slow pace of emissions cuts. Adão Soares Barbosa, chair of the Least Developed Countries group, said finance, adaptation and loss and damage are "matters of survival". Bowen also wants more attention on Pacific island nations, noting only 0.2 percent of available climate finance goes to small island states for adaptation.

The United States is sending no delegation for the second year in a row. A White House spokesperson said the administration wants no part of "extremist climate policies" embraced by other countries. A group of 20 Democratic members of Congress is attending.

Both host countries rely heavily on fossil fuels. Climate advocates and more than 500 Australian scientists say Australia should stop approving coalmines and gas projects. Turkey is pushing a target for 35 percent of global final energy to come from electricity by 2035, which faces opposition from some countries. UN climate chief Simon Stiell said almost every major economy now sees climate action as a driver of growth, jobs and secure energy.

More than 200,000 people marched through Amsterdam on Sunday in the "Red Line" protest, according to the Dutch branch of Amnesty International, one of the organisers. Al Jazeera reports that many marchers wore red and called for tighter trade restrictions on Israel and a halt to all arms sales. A busy street was closed to traffic for the march, and marchers echoed a man with a loudspeaker shouting "Free, free Palestine!"
Marcher Mike van Dongen told Al Jazeera that what is happening in Gaza is "inhumane". Of the Dutch authorities he said: "They are doing nothing. They don't dare take any serious steps."

Al Jazeera says at least 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, including 21,000 children, since October 2023. A ceasefire took effect on October 10 last year, but the outlet reports that Israeli attacks and killings have continued almost daily. Sunday's march resembled one in early October last year, which followed "Red Line" demonstrations in The Hague last June.

The war has strained Dutch-Israeli relations. Al Jazeera reports that the Dutch foreign minister resigned last year after failing to secure new sanctions against Israel. A new minority coalition government took office in February and introduced an import ban on products from Israeli settlements, which the Dutch government and most of the international community consider illegal. Al Jazeera says the ban caused a diplomatic spat with Israel.

Prime Minister Rob Jetten, who joined a march last year but was not at Sunday's, defended his government at his weekly news conference on Friday. He said: "Every single day and every single week, we do what we can to alleviate the terrible situation there." He added that his administration is "exerting greater political and diplomatic pressure" on Israel to abide by its agreements on Gaza.

Ministers are expected this week to make steep cuts to the UK government's electric vehicle targets, the Guardian reports, citing government sources. Louise Haigh, described as the de facto deputy prime minister, will finalise the plan after a meeting in Downing Street on Wednesday. She is expected to cut a 2030 sales target by about a quarter, a move that would relieve carmakers but alarm many Labour MPs.

Under the existing zero emission vehicle mandate, brought in by the last Conservative government, the share of EV sales required rises to 80 percent by 2030, with only EVs sold by 2035. The Guardian says the policy is expected to deliver nearly 14 percent of the emissions cuts the UK has pledged between 2028 and 2032. A consultation launched in August set out five options, from keeping 80 percent to cutting the interim target to 50 percent. Government insiders say Haigh will probably choose about 60 percent and extend flexibilities until 2034.

Ministers are divided. Business secretary Jonathan Reynolds wants 50 percent, transport secretary Heidi Alexander is believed to want about 60 percent, and energy-side ministers are understood to want 80 percent. Andy Burnham has recused himself because his wife advises the board of an EV charging network.

Carmakers say the interim targets are unattainable. The SMMT says battery EVs made up 26.6 percent of new car sales in the first 10 months of the year, against a 33 percent target. Labour MPs including Lizzi Collinge and Catherine Fookes want the mandate kept, and ChargeUK warned that weakening it puts £1.7bn of charging investment at risk.

A government spokesperson said no decisions have been taken, and that the government remains committed to the mandate, a 2030 phaseout of petrol and diesel-only new cars and 100 percent zero emission sales by 2035.
